notes:
I've put together notes for every verse from about a dozen classic and modern sources. I couldn't find anything usable from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, catholic.com, oca.org, or from current Lutheran, Pentecostal or Anglican teachers writing as such. So the "other views" come mainly from Augustine (Catholic, on newadvent.org), the Got Questions article on v. 15, and notes on old translations quoted by the classic commentators. Real disagreement between Protestant traditions shows up mostly at vv. 8–11 and v. 15.

**Background**
- Psalms 105 and 106 are a pair. This one praises God's faithfulness and leaves Israel's failures for the next psalm. Guzik, quoting another writer: they show "the two sides of the relation between God and His people". https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/
- Matthew Henry notes that vv. 1–11 also open the psalm David gave Asaph for temple worship once the ark was settled (1 Chronicles 16). Source. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_105.cfm
- The key word of the psalm is "He." Repeated again and again, it keeps attention on God's constant activity in everything His people went through. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-105.cfm

**v. 1:** "Call upon His name" probably means calling on the LORD rather than the idols of the nations. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/ The Pulpit Commentary takes "the nations" to mean the heathen peoples, so Israel is told to make God known to outsiders. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html Maclaren says this verse shows the singer knew why Israel had received so many mercies: to be the world's evangelist. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/105.htm Augustine (Catholic) points out that this psalm opens with "Hallelujah" and reads "give thanks"/"confess" here as praise. Source. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801105.htm

**v. 2:** The songs are to be sung to God, not to an audience or just for one's own enjoyment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/ Pulpit: people who are full of gratitude can't help talking about God's goodness when they speak with others. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html

**v. 3:** Pulpit: worldly people boast in strength and riches, but God's people boast in God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html Guzik quotes VanGemeren's three purposes of praise. Praise magnifies the LORD, deepens appreciation of the history of redemption, and is a witness to outsiders. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/

**v. 4:**
- God's people seek both God and His strength. Guzik links this to Ephesians 6:10, "be strong in the Lord". https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/
- Matthew Henry notes that several ancient versions read "Seek the Lord and be strengthened". That strength comes from God through faith and prayer. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_105.cfm
- Barnes: God's "face" means His favour, His smile on us. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-105.html
- Augustine asks how God can always be sought if He is ever found. His answer: faith has already found Him, hope still seeks Him, and love seeks to see Him face to face, when the search will end. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801105.htm

**v. 5:** God's people are always in danger of forgetting, and will drift that way unless they make a point of remembering. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/ Pulpit: the "judgments" are God's sentences on sinners, such as the Egyptians and the Canaanites. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html

**v. 6:** Pulpit: "chosen ones" is plural, so it refers to Jacob's children, not to Jacob himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html Maclaren: these family titles are the reason Israel must obey the earlier commands; being God's people gives them both the duty and the honour of praising Him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/105.htm

**v. 7:** Before turning to Israel, the psalm reminds us that God rules all the earth; His special covenant with Israel does not shrink His lordship over everyone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/ Pulpit: His laws apply everywhere and claim the obedience of all people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html

**v. 8:**
- Calling the covenant "the word He commanded" puts the stress on God's initiative, so this bond is by grace, not mutual bargaining. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/
- Barnes: "a thousand generations" means very many generations; in effect, always. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-105.html
- Spurgeon's collection: "remember" is used because a divine promise does not go out of date with time. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps105.cfm
- Maclaren: the three words covenant, word and oath are stacked up to make the promise feel as firm as possible; God swears by Himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/105.htm

**v. 9:** Pulpit: the covenant was made with Abraham in Genesis 15. The oath was first sworn to Abraham (Genesis 22:16) and repeated to Isaac (Genesis 26:3). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html

**v. 10:** Pulpit: it was confirmed to Jacob at Bethel (Genesis 28:13) and again after he was renamed Israel (Genesis 35:12). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html

**v. 11:** Pulpit: "portion" literally means the measuring line or cord of an inheritance. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html Spurgeon's collection: the shift from "you" (singular) to "your" (plural) shows the covenant was made with the whole people, though God spoke it to only a few. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps105.cfm

**Where readings differ on vv. 8–11 (the "everlasting" covenant and the land)**
- **Calvary Chapel / dispensational (Guzik):** The covenant is everlasting, and Israel's role as God's covenant people lasts until the end of the age. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/
- **Matthew Henry (Presbyterian):** the promise of Canaan was a type, a picture ahead of time, of the promise of eternal life in Christ to all believers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/105-22.html
- **Augustine (Catholic):** an earthly inheritance can't be everlasting, and the Old Testament covenant is replaced by the New. So the everlasting covenant here must be the covenant of justification and eternal inheritance that God promised to faith. "A thousand generations" stands for all generations. Source, source. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801105.htm
- **Ellicott:** reads the psalm as teaching that keeping the Promised Land depends on obeying the covenant God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-105.html

**v. 12:** Pulpit: "few in number" is literally "men of number", meaning easily counted: a few dozen, or a few hundred with their households. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html

**v. 13:** Pulpit traces Abraham's moves from Ur to Haran, Canaan, Philistia and Egypt. Chaldea, Philistia and Egypt were "kingdoms"; the Syrians and Canaanites were "peoples". https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html

**v. 14:** The kings rebuked were Pharaoh (Genesis 12:17) and Abimelech of Gerar (Genesis 20). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html Maclaren: the little band of wanderers looked vulnerable, but God was their "shield". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/105.htm

**v. 15:**
- **Traditional reading:** "Anointed ones" is plural. It means people set apart for God's service, as Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were. These exact words don't appear in Genesis, but they express the lesson God's dealings with Pharaoh and Abimelech taught. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/105-15.htm
- The patriarchs were never literally anointed. Ellicott: the title still fits, because it is sometimes used for the covenant people as a whole. Source. Abraham is called a prophet in Genesis 20:7. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/105-15.htm
- **Barnes (Presbyterian):** this is the voice of God's providence, a poetic way of describing it, not words spoken aloud. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/105-15.html
- **Calvin (Reformed):** God defended them not just because they were wronged, but because He had freely adopted them and promised to maintain them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/105-15.html
- **Clarke (Methodist):** Perhaps the whole people of Israel is meant, as a kingdom of priests and kings. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/105-15.html
- **Gill (Baptist):** applies the verse to all true believers, anointed with the Holy Spirit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/105-15.html
- **Maclaren:** "every Christian is a Messiah" and a prophet. The harm God protects them from is real harm, not "so-called evil". https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/105-15.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** God's prophets are anointed with the Spirit. Even people who kill the prophets cannot do them any real harm. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_105.cfm
- **Augustine (Catholic):** God's words to the kings were spoken secretly in their hearts through visions, or through an angel. He also asks whether the patriarchs were called "christs" because they were already Christians in secret. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801105.htm
- **Debated popular use:** Got Questions notes that the verse is sometimes used in Pentecostal and Charismatic circles to defend certain preachers from criticism. Others take it to promise that Christians will be protected from everything bad. Got Questions rejects both readings: the "anointed ones" are not modern preachers, and the Bible never promises believers won't suffer. https://www.gotquestions.org/touch-not-Gods-anointed.html
- **A different modern note:** BibleHub's study note does apply the verse to honouring today's faithful teachers, pastors and missionaries. https://biblehub.com/psalms/105-15.htm

**v. 16:** Pulpit: what God "calls for" comes into being at once. Bread is called a "staff" because it holds up life. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html Augustine rejects the idea of famine as a person or god. "Called" just means God commanded it. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801105.htm Henry: the famine tested the patriarchs, showing that God had a better country in mind for them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_105.cfm

**v. 17:** God ordained the injustice done to Joseph so he could be sent ahead to save the family. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/ Augustine: the sale was the brothers' sin, yet God sent Joseph. God uses men's evil deeds well. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801105.htm Keil & Delitzsch point to Joseph's own words in Genesis 45:5. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/105-18.htm

**v. 18:**
- **The translation question:** the old Prayer Book line "the iron entered into his soul" is famous, but the parallel lines favour "he was laid in iron". The Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation) reads "his soul passed through iron". The Latin Vulgate has "the iron passed through his soul". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/105-18.htm
- The Cambridge Bible questions the Prayer Book rendering on grammatical grounds, but says the sense is much the same: Joseph keenly felt his unjust imprisonment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/105-18.htm
- Calvin: whichever reading, the meaning is the same. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/105-18.html
- Augustine: "soul" points to his inner anguish. He compares Simeon's words to Mary in Luke 2:35. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801105.htm
- Gill (Baptist): Joseph here is a type of Christ, who was bound. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/105-18.htm
- F.B. Meyer, quoted by Guzik: a soft lad came out of prison fit to govern Egypt. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/

**v. 19:**
- **Pulpit:** Joseph's word "came true" when the butler was restored. It is hard to say which "word of the LORD" is meant; one suggestion is the implied promise in his dreams. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** "his word" is Joseph's account of his visions, and God's word was a promise that had to try, prove and purify him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/105-18.htm
- **Spurgeon's collection:** his faith in the promise was tested by the long imprisonment, which was a divine discipline preparing him for its fulfilment. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps105.cfm
- **Readings closer to BSB's "proved him right":**
  - A translator's note in Calvin's commentary (quoting Street): the verb means refining metal. Applied to metal already pure, it showed him to be innocent. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/105-19.html
  - Matthew Henry: the word of the LORD "cleared him". His God-given power to foretell events rolled away the reproach of the false charge. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_105.cfm

**v. 20:** Pulpit: Pharaoh made him a free man instead of a prisoner and slave (Genesis 41:14). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html Calvin: God's unusual power was clearly on show in something so unlikely. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom11/calcom11.xiv.v.html

**v. 21:** Pulpit cites Genesis 41:40. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html Henry describes Joseph's offices as chamberlain, treasurer and prime minister. Source. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_105.cfm

**v. 22:**
- **Translation note:** the Hebrew and the King James have "bind his princes". The BSB's "instruct" matches the Latin Vulgate ("erudiret"), Luther's German and the Peshitta (the Syriac translation). Source. https://biblehub.com/multi/psalms/105-22.htm
- **Pulpit:** Joseph, as Pharaoh's stand-in, could imprison anyone. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html
- **Calvin and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** "bind" means control and the duty to obey, not literal chains. JFB: the soul once bound now binds princes. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom11/calcom11.xiv.v.html, https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_105.cfm
- **Spurgeon:** "He who was bound obtains authority to bind." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps105.cfm
- **Barnes:** "senators" is a misleading translation. The word means aged counsellors. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/105-22.htm
- **Gill (Baptist):** applies it to Christ, whose "senators" are his apostles and ministers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/105-22.htm
- **Augustine:** neither the fetters nor this teaching are recorded in Genesis. He assumes the Holy Spirit knew what the history left out. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801105.htm

**Joseph as a picture of Christ (vv. 17–22):** Matthew Henry: at the appointed time Christ was exalted as Mediator. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/105-22.htm Spurgeon's collection compares Joseph's story to the Christian's: election, redemption, and justification. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps105.cfm
